title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani close

lines: A MONTH WITH THE NINTH GURU.
BEFORE WE TURN TO THE ARDAS.
cards: If you had to describe a teacher in four words after a month with them, what would you pick? Not their biography. The feel of them: the voice you'd hear in your head when you needed it.
We started this block on the ninth Guru's voice, calm and plain. Since then we've walked through his shabads in their ragas and all fifty-seven saloks. A wall of sand.
Friends in good times. Kanchan. Fear none, frighten none.
Auadh. Rama gone, Ravana gone. Strength gone, strength returned.

teach.b: The four words are calm, fearless, detached, and kind. Calm. His bani has almost no drama in it.
Short lines, plain words, the same truths said again and again: live in the world, shining, like a dream, auadh. It reads like someone speaking slowly to a friend who is upset. Fearless.
The salok we met as fear none, frighten none says, in paraphrase, that the wise one gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one. Sikhs see that line lived out in his death.

Tradition remembers that he went to Delhi and gave his life in 1675, and Sikhs honor him as having died for others' freedom to practice their own faith. He's often called Hind di chadar, the shield of India. Detached.

The word in his bani is often bairaag, a turning away from clutching, and the picture is kanchan and iron alike, praise and blame alike. Not cold, but unhooked: love without clutching, as one day's line had it. Kind.

This one is easy to miss, because his bani talks so much about death. But all that talk of passing is never meant to frighten. It's said the way you'd tell someone you love: we don't have forever, so let's not waste it.
Strength gone, then strength returned. All companions gone, then rahio.
Every hard line turns, sooner or later, toward what stays.
That's the ninth Guru's bani: fifty-nine shabads in fifteen ragas, and fifty-seven saloks, most of them two lines long. Small in size. Not small in weight.

how: Sikhs hear Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads in kirtan and his saloks at every bhog, and on the day of his martyrdom, often observed in November or December, gurdwaras sing his bani and tell the story of Delhi.

o: without fear, one of four words for his bani
without home, a wanderer with no fixed place
without anger, never raising one's voice

games.q: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani — tap the pairs.
p: every hard line turns to what stays

s: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani is fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks
fifty-nine shabads in fifteen ragas, and fifty-seven saloks.
his talk of death is meant to frighten
it's said the way you'd tell someone you love: we don't have forever.
detached in his bani means cold
it means unhooked: love without clutching, gold and iron alike.

games.q: a month of the ninth Guru's bani is done. the practice asks you to carry one salok this week. how do you choose?
o: the one that tugs at you.
games.why: the practice says don't choose the wisest; choose the one that catches, and carry it.

practice: Let a few of this month's lines pass through your mind: live in the world, shining; like a dream; nothing stays; today or tomorrow; only you; the Name remains; nothing equals it.
Don't choose the wisest; notice the one that tugs, and say it three times, slowly, with your breath. If you pray, follow it with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Nirbhau, without fear. One of four words for his bani: calm, nirbhau, detached, and kind: fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks, small in size, not small in weight.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirbhau, without fear; a word from the Mool Mantar that Sikhs see lived out in the ninth Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: calm and fearless. Tomorrow, the prayer said standing. Day six hundred ten, and a whole block done.
